title: Two-Stage Op Amps
intro: When one stage cannot give both the gain and the swing, split the jobs: a first stage for gain and a common-source second stage for swing (Razavi, Sections 9.3, 9.6 and 9.7.4).

blocks.text: Telescopic and folded cascodes convert voltage to current once, so their gain is $G_m R_{out}$ and every cascode that raises $R_{out}$ eats swing. With a 0.9 V supply and a required 0.8 V single-ended swing, no cascode stack fits. A two-stage op amp isolates the requirements: the first stage provides gain, and the second, a simple common-source stage, swings to within one overdrive of each rail.

blocks.alt: Fully differential two-stage op amp. An NMOS differential pair M1, M2 with tail ISS has PMOS current-source loads M3, M4 biased by Vb1. Their drains, X and Y, drive the gates of PMOS common-source transistors M5 and M6, whose NMOS current-source loads M7 and M8 are biased by Vb2. The outputs Vout1 and Vout2 are at the drains of M5/M7 and M6/M8.
blocks.caption: A fully differential two-stage op amp. Common-mode feedback and compensation are not shown.

blocks.tex: A_v = g_{m1,2}(r_{O1,2} \parallel r_{O3,4}) \cdot g_{m5,6}(r_{O5,6} \parallel r_{O7,8}), \qquad V_{out,pp} = V_{DD} - |V_{OD5,6}| - V_{OD7,8} \text{ per side}

blocks.text: For more gain, cascode the first stage. Because the second stage has a gain of 10 or so, the swing at X and Y is small, so the first stage can be optimized for gain alone:

A single-ended output can be made by keeping the first stage differential and converting the two second-stage currents with a current mirror. More than two stages is rare: each stage adds at least one pole, and stability becomes hard to guarantee (multipath and nested-Miller schemes exist for that).

Split the power between the stages. Design the output stage first: its swing sets the overdrives (for example 0.2 V and 0.3 V for the two output devices). Give the larger overdrive to the current-source device: a small overdrive on the current source raises its noise current, and the signal device wants high $g_m = 2I_D/V_{OD}$. That makes the signal device wide, which adds capacitance at X and Y. Then the first stage: because $V_{DS3,4} = |V_{GS5,6}|$, the second stage fixes the first stage's operating point and its allowed overdrives. Keep the input pair's overdrive small (high $g_m$, low noise; at very low overdrive it enters subthreshold, where $g_m \approx I_D/(\xi V_T)$), and the load devices' overdrive large so they contribute less noise than the input pair.

In nanometer devices the saturation-triode boundary is blurry, so do not judge swing from bias points. Instead apply sinusoids of growing amplitude in simulation and plot the gain against output amplitude; the swing is the amplitude where the gain has dropped by an accepted amount (for example 10%, about 1 dB). If distortion is what matters, put the op amp in its closed-loop configuration and find the amplitude at which the harmonics become unacceptable.
Common-mode feedback in two-stage op amps
Both stages have high-impedance, current-defined outputs, so both need their CM level defined (see the Common-Mode Feedback page for the basics). Three options:

items: Sense the output CM and correct only the second stage (its current sources): nothing defines X and Y. If $I_{SS}$ is less than what $M_3$ and $M_4$ want, X and Y rise until $M_3$, $M_4$ fall into triode, which also cuts $|V_{GS5,6}|$ and the second-stage current. Not usable.

Sense the output CM and correct the first stage (for example $I_{SS}$): if the outputs are high, the error amplifier cuts $I_{SS}$, X and Y rise, $M_5$-$M_6$ conduct less and the outputs fall. It works because $M_5$ and $M_6$ themselves sense the CM at X and Y. But the CM loop now passes the pole at X, the output pole, the error amplifier's pole and a pole from the large sensing resistors with the error amplifier's input capacitance: three or four poles, hard to stabilize.

Use two separate local loops, one per stage. A neat version: resistors $R_1$, $R_2$ between X and Y with their midpoint driving the gates of the PMOS loads, so the loads act as current sources for differential signals and as diodes for CM; $M_5$, $M_6$ then mirror their currents. Resistors $R_3$, $R_4$ across the outputs do the same for the NMOS output loads. Gain $g_{m1}(r_{O1} \parallel r_{O3} \parallel R_1)\,g_{m5}(r_{O5} \parallel r_{O7} \parallel R_3)$.

blocks.text: In that last scheme the output CM sits at the output NMOS devices' $V_{GS}$, a little above a threshold, well below mid-supply. Drawing a small current $I_Q$ from the midpoint of $R_3$, $R_4$ shifts the output CM up by $R_3 I_Q/2$. With a cascoded first stage, sense the CM near (not at) X and Y so the sensing does not load the high-impedance nodes.

Two-stage op amps must also be compensated (Miller compensation with pole splitting) and they slew at a rate set by the first-stage current and the compensation capacitor; see Stability and Frequency Compensation. To raise the gain of a one-stage op amp without a second stage, see Gain Boosting.

blocks.title: Two-stage gain
blocks.text: Stage one has $g_{m1} = 1$ mS and output resistance $50\text{ k}\Omega \parallel 50\text{ k}\Omega$. Stage two has $g_{m6} = 2$ mS and output resistance 25 k$\Omega$. Find the total gain.

blocks.title: Swing comparison
blocks.text: At $V_{DD} = 1.2$ V, compare the per-side swing of a two-stage op amp whose output devices have overdrives of 0.2 V (PMOS) and 0.15 V (NMOS) with a telescopic op amp whose five stacked devices each have 0.15 V.
solution: Two-stage: $1.2 - 0.2 - 0.15 = 0.85\text{ V}_{pp}$ per side, 1.7 V differential.
Telescopic: $1.2 - 5 \times 0.15 = 0.45\text{ V}_{pp}$ per side, 0.9 V differential.

blocks.title: Designing for gain
blocks.text: A two-stage design has a first stage with $g_{m1} = 2$ mS and $r_{O1} \parallel r_{O3} = 20\text{ k}\Omega$, and a second stage with $g_{m5} = 4$ mS and $r_{O5} \parallel r_{O7} = 5\text{ k}\Omega$. What is the gain? If all lengths in the first stage are doubled at the same overdrive and current, what is it then?
solution: Doubling $L$ (and $W$) leaves $g_m$ unchanged and doubles $r_O$, so the first stage gives 80 and the total 1600 (64 dB), at the cost of more capacitance at X and Y.

blocks.title: The broken CMFB option
blocks.text: In a fully differential two-stage op amp, CMFB senses the outputs and adjusts only the output-stage NMOS current sources. The tail current is 2% below what the PMOS loads $M_3$, $M_4$ try to supply. What happens?
solution: No loop defines the CM level at X and Y. With the loads supplying more than the tail sinks, X and Y rise until $M_3$, $M_4$ enter triode and their current drops to $I_{SS}/2$ each.
Then $|V_{GS5,6}|$ is smaller than designed, so the second stage runs at a much lower current than intended, regardless of what the output CMFB does.
blocks.answer: X and Y float up and starve the second stage; the first stage needs its own CM control.
